46.modern-en: The captive remains in the reunited company as the curate's scheme to cage Don Quixote is set in motion.

47.modern-en: The captain embraces the curate and barber in farewell and rides on with his brother, Zoraida, and Don Fernando's party towards Andalusia.

epithet.en: The Algerian noblewoman who converts to Christianity and escapes with the Captive
epithet.da: Den algeriske adelsdame, der konverterer til kristendommen og flygter med den fangne

37.modern-en: Zoraida arrives veiled at the inn on the captive's arm, refusing the name Zoraida and insisting she be called Maria.

38.modern-en: Zoraida sits silently with the women through Don Quixote's discourse on arms and letters, still in her Moorish dress.

40.modern-en: Zoraida is revealed as author of the letters dropped into the captive's prison yard, a Moor's daughter taught to pray to Lela Marien.

41.modern-en: Zoraida meets the captive in her father's garden, boards the escape vessel with her trunk of gold, and watches her father cast ashore cursing her.

42.modern-en: Zoraida sits at the women's table with Luscinda and Dorothea as her captive's brother the Judge is recognised and the family reunited.

43.modern-en: Zoraida sleeps in the women's chamber through the night of the muleteer's singing and Doña Clara's tearful confession.

44.modern-en: Zoraida watches with the other ladies of the inn as the dispute over Don Luis and the pack-saddle plays out.

45.modern-en: Zoraida remains at the inn through the quarrel over Mambrino's helmet and the officers of the Holy Brotherhood.

46.modern-en: Zoraida is among the company that has now been two days at the inn, witness to the plan to cage Don Quixote.

47.modern-en: Zoraida says farewell to the curate and barber and rides on with the captive and his brother the Judge towards Andalusia.

epithet.en: The Aragonese aristocrat who, having read Part One, stages elaborate court jokes around Don Quixote
epithet.da: Den aragonske adelsmand, der efter at have læst Første Del iscenesætter omfattende hofspøg omkring Don Quixote

82.modern-en: The duke greets Don Quixote on his hunting ground, recognises him from the printed history, and escorts him to his castle resolved to indulge his chivalric fantasy in every detail.

83.modern-en: The duke orders his household to receive Don Quixote with the full ceremony of a knight-errant, insists he take the head of the table, and watches the ecclesiastic in his household scold his guest as a madman.

84.modern-en: The duke laughs at the ecclesiastic storming out, confers the governorship of an island on Sancho on the spot, and lets the damsels' farcical beard-washing pass without rebuke.

86.modern-en: The duke takes Don Quixote and Sancho hunting, then stages an elaborate night-time pageant of devils, sages, and the enchanted Dulcinea to feed the knight's delusions.

87.modern-en: The duke listens with satisfaction as his majordomo, playing Merlin, decrees that Sancho must lash himself three thousand three hundred times to disenchant Dulcinea.

88.modern-en: The duke welcomes the Distressed Duenna — his own majordomo in disguise as the Countess Trifaldi — and pledges Don Quixote's protection to her.

89.modern-en: The duke sides with Sancho's view that the household should go out to receive the visiting countess only insofar as she is a countess, keeping the elaborate joke moving.

93.modern-en: The duke assures Sancho that his promised island will still be waiting on his return from Clavileño's flight, then with the duchess plays dead in the garden as the firework horse explodes.

94.modern-en: The duke instructs Sancho to prepare for the governorship, tells him a governor's clothes must suit his office, and sends him off the next day to the island of Barataria.

97.modern-en: The duke receives by courier a full account of Sancho's first day on the bench at Barataria, eager to see how his joke is unfolding.

99.modern-en: The duke sends Sancho a letter at Barataria warning of imagined assassins and a plot to poison his food — another move in the running joke at the governor's expense.

102.modern-en: The duke gives the duchess leave to creep to Don Quixote's door with Altisidora, where they overhear Doña Rodriguez gossiping and burst in to flog the duenna and pinch the knight black and blue.

104.modern-en: The duke accepts Doña Rodriguez's challenge on behalf of his vassal, fixing six days hence for a formal trial by combat in his castle courtyard.

106.modern-en: The duke, his vassal having fled to Flanders, arranges for his lacquey Tosilos to fight Don Quixote in disguise and primes him on exactly how to behave.

107.modern-en: The duke and duchess receive the bruised and disgoverned Sancho back at the castle, embrace him, and promise him some lighter post on the estate.

108.modern-en: The duke instructs Tosilos to shirk the combat, then is astonished and angry when his lacquey, smitten with the daughter at first sight, yields and offers to marry her on the spot.

109.modern-en: The duke, keeping up the joke, accuses Don Quixote of stealing Altisidora's garters and challenges him to mortal combat before letting him ride away from the castle.

121.modern-en: The duke, having had the roads watched for Don Quixote's return, stages the elaborate spectacle of Altisidora's mock death and resurrection with Sancho's face-smacking and pinching as the cure.

122.modern-en: The duke and duchess pay Don Quixote a final visit in his chamber the morning after the resurrection joke, then let him take his departure that same day.

epithet.en: The duke's wife, who designs much of the cruel court entertainment at their expense
epithet.da: Hertugens hustru, der står bag meget af den ondsindede hofunderholdning på deres bekostning

82.modern-en: The duchess receives Sancho's chivalric message with delight on her hunting party, recognises him at once from the printed history, and welcomes Don Quixote to her country estate.

83.modern-en: The duchess keeps Sancho at her side for the pleasure of his rustic shrewdness, defends him when he insults Doña Rodriguez about the donkey, and sets the household to treat Don Quixote with full chivalric ceremony.

84.modern-en: The duchess presses Don Quixote to describe Dulcinea's beauty, draws him into a long discussion of her supposed enchantment, and indulges Sancho's beard-washing tantrum to her own amusement.

85.modern-en: The duchess gets Sancho alone and coaxes him into admitting he invented Dulcinea's enchantment, then turns it back on him by insisting his own enchanters were the real authors of the trick.

86.modern-en: The duchess takes the field with a boar-spear during the hunt, watches Sancho dangle from his torn green coat, and helps stage the night pageant of devils, sages, and Merlin.

87.modern-en: The duchess urges Sancho to consent to the three thousand three hundred lashes for Dulcinea's sake, leaning on his gratitude to his master.

88.modern-en: The duchess receives Sancho's letter to Teresa, finds him covetous and confused but lets the letter stand, then witnesses the entrance of the Distressed Duenna's squire Trifaldin.

89.modern-en: The duchess wonders whether to go out and meet the visiting countess, debating with Sancho about the standing of duennas.

90.modern-en: The duchess applauds the majordomo's clever acting as the Countess Trifaldi spins out her tale of the bearded duennas of Kandy.

92.modern-en: The duchess defends her own duennas against Sancho's tirade, then helps press him into agreeing to ride Clavileño to the rescue of the bearded countess.

93.modern-en: The duchess pretends to faint with the rest of the household when Clavileño explodes, then teases Sancho's tall tale of seeing the earth like a mustard seed from the sky.

94.modern-en: The duchess applauds the duke's continued joke as Sancho is fitted out to leave for the governorship of Barataria.

96.modern-en: The duchess plots a fresh trick when Altisidora reports Don Quixote's offer of music, then arranges the bell-and-cat fright for that night.

98.modern-en: The duchess, alerted by Altisidora and her companion, helps stage the bell-and-cat assault on Don Quixote's window and rushes in horrified when the joke draws blood.

100.modern-en: The duchess, tipped off that Doña Rodriguez has slipped into Don Quixote's chamber, listens at the door with Altisidora and bursts in to flog the gossiping duenna in silence.

102.modern-en: The duchess writes a familiar, generous letter to Teresa Panza praising her husband's governorship and sending her a string of gold-clasped coral beads.

103.modern-en: The duchess gives orders that Doña Rodriguez and her daughter are no longer to be treated as servants but as lady adventurers, then receives Teresa Panza's reply through her returning page.

107.modern-en: The duchess embraces the battered and disgoverned Sancho on his return to the castle and gives orders that he be cared for.

109.modern-en: The duchess is astonished by Altisidora's brazen farewell ballad accusing Don Quixote of stealing her garters, then promises to chastise her damsel as the knight rides off.

121.modern-en: The duchess takes her seat on the stage beside the duke to watch the staged resurrection of Altisidora through the smacking and pinching of Sancho.

122.modern-en: The duchess asks Don Quixote whether Altisidora is in his good graces and, on his advice, promises to keep her damsel busy with needlework as a cure for her supposed love-sickness.

epithet.en: The duchess's damsel who feigns hopeless love for Don Quixote and later her own death
epithet.da: Hertugindens kammerpige, der spiller håbløst forelsket i Don Quixote og senere sin egen død

96.modern-en: Altisidora stages a sighing scene under Don Quixote's grated window and sings a ballad declaring herself a love-stricken virgin of fourteen burning for the Manchegan knight.

98.modern-en: Altisidora pretends to faint in the gallery to draw Don Quixote into asking for a lute, then bandages his cat-scratched face that night while whispering that his cruelty has earned him the wounds.

109.modern-en: Altisidora delivers a brazen mock-tragic farewell ballad as Don Quixote rides out of the castle, accusing him of stealing three kerchiefs and her garters before confessing she was wearing the garters all along.

121.modern-en: Altisidora lies as the lovely corpse on the catafalque at the duke's castle while a Roman-clad poet sings her death, and revives only after Sancho has been smacked, pricked, and pinched by duennas.

122.modern-en: Altisidora enters Don Quixote's chamber the morning after her resurrection to reproach him, then drops the act when he again refuses her and calls him Don Stockfish before sweeping out.

epithet.en: The settled country gentleman in the green coat who hosts Don Quixote for several quiet chapters
epithet.da: Den bofaste landherre i den grønne kappe, der huser Don Quixote i flere stille kapitler

68.modern-en: Don Diego de Miranda overtakes Don Quixote on the road in his green gaban, describes his quiet country life and his poet son, and listens with growing puzzlement to the knight's speeches.

69.modern-en: Don Diego watches in horror as Don Quixote insists on facing the caged lion, tries to dissuade him, then concludes he is a sane man gone mad and a madman on the verge of sanity.

70.modern-en: Don Diego brings Don Quixote home to meet his wife Doña Cristina and his student son Don Lorenzo, hosts him lavishly for four days, and watches his guest oscillate between sense and nonsense before sending him on his way.

epithet.en: The galley-slave Don Quixote freed in Part One, returning in Part Two as a fugitive puppet-showman
epithet.da: Galejslaven, Don Quixote befriede i Første Del, der vender tilbage i Anden Del som flygtende dukkemand

22.modern-en: Ginés de Pasamonte, the most heavily chained and defiant of the galley slaves, boasts of his unfinished autobiography, accepts Don Quixote's rescue, then leads the freed prisoners in stoning their deliverer and stripping him of his coat.

23.modern-en: Ginés, hiding from the Holy Brotherhood in the Sierra Morena, recognises the sleeping pair and steals Sancho's donkey Dapple before dawn — the famous textual crux Cervantes leaves unexplained until Part Two.

30.modern-en: Ginés reappears disguised as a gypsy riding the stolen Dapple; Sancho recognises him at once, shouts him down as 'Ginesillo, you thief,' and Ginés leaps off and bolts, leaving the donkey behind.

56.modern-en: Sancho complains to Sansón Carrasco that the printed history has muddled the donkey theft, naming Ginés de Pasamonte as 'the great rogue and rascal' who stole Dapple — the in-novel acknowledgment of Cervantes's blunder.

77.modern-en: A one-eyed puppet-showman calling himself Master Pedro arrives at the inn with a divining ape, recognises Don Quixote and Sancho at once, and astounds them by 'divining' details of their lives through the ape.

78.modern-en: Master Pedro stages his puppet-show of the rescue of Melisendra, narrated by a boy interpreter whom he repeatedly corrects from inside the booth — until Don Quixote rises sword in hand and hacks the Moorish puppets to pieces.

79.modern-en: Cide Hamete unmasks Master Pedro as Ginés de Pasamonte himself, in disguise and on the run from justice, surviving by puppet-shows and the trick of researching each village before pretending the ape divines its secrets.

epithet.en: The historical Catalan bandit chief who briefly hosts Don Quixote on the road to Barcelona
epithet.da: Den historiske catalanske banditchef, der kort huser Don Quixote på vejen til Barcelona

112.modern-en: Roque Guinart, the Catalan bandit captain, surrounds Don Quixote and Sancho near Barcelona, stops his men from robbing Sancho's girdle, and — recognising Don Quixote's madness as more pitiable than dangerous — receives them with surprising courtesy.

113.modern-en: Roque shelters Don Quixote and Sancho for three restless days among his band, then escorts them by secret paths to the Barcelona shore at dawn, presses ten promised crowns into Sancho's hand, and turns them over to a friend who welcomes them into the city.
